```{r data}
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forecast)
library(fpp2)
library(TTR)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(car)
library(psych) 
library(corrplot)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(tinytex)
data <- read_csv("ecdc_covid19_cases_2020.csv")
covid_19 <- na.omit(data) 
```


```{r descriptive statistics}
# 1) Descriptive Statistics
summary(covid_19)
summary(covid_19$cases)
quantile((covid_19$cases))
summary(covid_19$deaths)
quantile((covid_19$deaths))
summary(covid_19$`Cumulative_number_for_14_days_of_COVID-19_cases_per_100000`)
quantile((covid_19$`Cumulative_number_for_14_days_of_COVID-19_cases_per_100000`))




```
***The summary statistics for the COVID-19 dataset display summary values for the dataset's attributes. The numeric variables are divided into four quarters with the 1st quartile displaying the 25th percentile with 25% of the data points contained below Q1.The 2nd quartile displays the median values for the dataset's variables with 50% of the datapoints contained below Q2 and 50% of the datapoints contained above Q2.The 3rd quartile contains 75% of the datapoints below Q3 and 25% of the datapoints above Q3. The interquartile range contains the middle 50% of the datapoints distribution. The median value for the cases variable is 20 and the 3rd quartile value is 312. Thus for the cases variable, the middle value is 20 with values +-20 contained in the area 50% below 20 and 50% above 20. All values above 312 are contained in the 25% area above this value for the 3rd quartile. The median value for the deaths variable is 0 and the 3rd quartile value is 5. Thus for the deaths variable, the middle value is 0 with values +-0 contained in the area 50% below 20 and 50% above 20. All values above 5 are contained in the 25% area above this value for the 3rd quartile. Of note, the average value for the deaths variable is 27.44. The median value for the Cumulative_number_for_14_days_of_COVID-19_cases_per_100000 variable is 6.699 and the 3rd quartile value is 52.618. Thus for the Cumulative_number_for_14_days_of_COVID-19_cases_per_100000 variable, the middle value is 6.699 with values +-6.699 contained in the area 50% below 6.699 and 50% above 6.699. All values above 52.618 are contained in the 25% area above this value for the 3rd quartile.*** 

```{r incidence_rate}
range <- function(x) {max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)}
Global_incidence_rate <- range((covid_19$cases / covid_19$popData2019) * 100000)
Global_fatality_rate <- (range(covid_19$deaths) / range(covid_19$cases)) 
print(list('Global Incidence Rate:', Global_incidence_rate, 'Global Fatality Rate:', Global_fatality_rate))
```
***The global incidence rate for COVID-19 is 1,084.05 which represents the daily total number of COVID-19 cases reported per 100,000 people. The global fatality rate for COVID-19 is 2.819% which represents the percentage of COVID-19 reported cases resulting in death.***

## Including Visualizations

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r plots, echo=TRUE}
scatterplot(covid_19$month, covid_19$cases, main="COVID-19 Cases", 
   xlab="Month", ylab="COVID-19 Cases", pch=19)
scatterplot(covid_19$month, covid_19$deaths, main="COVID-19 Deaths", 
   xlab="Month", ylab="COVID-19 Deaths", pch=19)
```
***The first scatter plot visualizes the aggregated count of cases for COVID-19 during 2020. Between the second and fourth months of 2020, the number of cases tripled. Between the fourth and sixth months of 2020, the number of cases slightly increased but the largest increases in cases occurred in the eleventh month by doubling from the amount of cases which occurred in month ten. The aggregated total count for cases during 2020 was 234,633 reflecting the maximum value for the cases variable. The second scatter plot visualizes the aggregated count of deaths for COVID-19 during 2020. The maximum fatality value occurred during the fourth month of 2020 with a total value of 4,928 deaths. The seventh, eight, and ninth months saw a consistent value of nearly 4,000 deaths per month.***

```{r Inferential Statistics, echo=TRUE}
# 2). Inferential Statistics
Canada <- covid_19 %>%
  filter(countriesAndTerritories == "Canada") %>%
  print()
USA <- covid_19 %>%
  filter(countriesAndTerritories == "United_States_of_America") %>%
  print()
Canada_incidence_rate <- range((Canada$cases / Canada$popData2019) * 100000)
USA_incidence_rate <- range((USA$cases / USA$popData2019) * 100000) 
Two_Countries_Incidence_test <- t.test((USA$cases / USA$popData2019) * 100000, (Canada$cases / Canada$popData2019) * 100000, alternative="two.sided")
Two_Countries_Incidence_test
print(list('USA Incidence Rate:', USA_incidence_rate, 'Canada Incidence Rate:', Canada_incidence_rate))

```
***The null hypothesis is that no significant difference exist between the mean of the groups. The alternative hypothesis is that a significant difference exist between the mean of the groups. The average incidence rate for both groups is between 9.24 and 12.76 with a 95% confidence interval. As the p-value is smaller than 0.05, the results are statistically significant and the null hypothesis is rejected. The alternative hypothesis is accepted that there exist a significant difference between the mean of the groups for incidence rate.***

```{r Continued Inferential Statistics, echo=TRUE}
Canada_fatality_rate <- (range(Canada$deaths) / range(Canada$cases)) 
USA_fatality_rate <- (range(USA$deaths) / range(USA$cases))
Two_Countries_Fatality_test <- t.test((Canada$deaths / Canada$cases), (USA$deaths / USA$cases), alternative="two.sided")
Two_Countries_Fatality_test 
print(list('USA Fataility Rate:', USA_fatality_rate, 'Canada Fatality Rate:', Canada_fatality_rate))
```
***The null hypothesis is that no significant difference exist between the mean of the groups. The alternative hypothesis is that a significant difference exist between the mean of the groups. The average incidence rate for both groups is between 0.0383 and 0.0165 with a 95% confidence interval. As the p-value is smaller than 0.05, the results are statistically significant and the null hypothesis is rejected. The alternative hypothesis is accepted that there exist a significant difference between the mean of the groups for fatality rates.***

```{r Rate Plots, echo=TRUE}
ggplot(data = covid_19, aes(x = month, y = cases)) + geom_point(aes(color = Global_incidence_rate), size = .1) + ggtitle("COVID-19 Global Case Rate")
ggplot(data = covid_19, aes(x = deaths, y = cases)) + geom_point(aes(color = Global_fatality_rate), size = .1) + ggtitle("COVID-19 Global Fatality Rate")
ggplot(data = covid_19, aes(x = Global_incidence_rate, y = Global_fatality_rate)) + geom_point(aes(color = deaths), size = 2, shape = 23) + ggtitle("COVID-19 Incidence & Fatality Rates")
```


```{r coefficients, echo=TRUE}
model <- lm(cases ~ popData2019 + deaths + countriesAndTerritories, data=covid_19)
summary(model)
plot(model) 
```
***The correlation coefficient is 0.623. This indicates a moderate positive linear relationship between the variables.The regression predictions move in the same direction and fit the data and indicate a strong correlation at a global level.***

```{r time series, echo=TRUE}
model_cases <- auto.arima(covid_19$cases)
forecast(model_cases,5)
model_deaths <- auto.arima(covid_19$deaths)
forecast(model_deaths,5)


```
Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.
